title: Joins: outer, self, semi and anti
summary: Every join type as row matching rather than Venn circles: INNER, LEFT/RIGHT, FULL and CROSS; ON versus WHERE for outer joins; one-to-many fan-out that inflates sums; self joins for pairs and hierarchies; semi and anti joins with EXISTS, NOT EXISTS and the NOT IN NULL trap; USING, multi-column keys and why NULL keys never match.
prerequisiteNotes: sql-select-basics: SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY with COUNT/SUM, and three-valued logic (NULL = NULL is unknown, WHERE keeps only true). Every join gotcha in this lesson is one of those rules meeting a NULL-padded or repeated row.
objectives: Predict the exact rows an INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL or CROSS join returns by matching rows, including unmatched and NULL-key rows.
Place a right-table filter in ON rather than WHERE so a LEFT JOIN keeps its unmatched rows, and count them with `count(right.id)`.
Spot one-to-many fan-out and fix inflated sums by aggregating before joining.
Write self joins for hierarchies and for unordered pairs using `a.id < b.id`.
Write semi and anti joins with EXISTS and NOT EXISTS, and explain why NOT IN returns nothing when the subquery yields a NULL.
Choose between ON and USING, join on composite keys, and say what happens to NULL keys.

concepts.title: Joins match rows; they are not Venn diagrams
concepts.body: A join pairs every row of the left input with every row of the right input for which the ON condition is **true**, and emits one output row per pair. That is all `INNER JOIN` does. Venn circles hide the two facts interviews probe: a left row with three matches appears **three times**, and a row whose key is NULL matches nothing. The outer joins add back unmatched rows padded with NULLs: `LEFT JOIN` keeps unmatched left rows, `RIGHT JOIN` unmatched right rows (it is a LEFT JOIN with the tables swapped; most teams write only LEFT), and `FULL JOIN` both. `CROSS JOIN` has no condition and returns every combination, so 1,000 × 1,000 rows is a million, and crossing with an empty table returns **zero** rows. Before writing a join, say the **grain** of the result: "one row per customer" or "one row per order line".
concepts.code:
-- customers: Ana(1), Ben(2), Cy(3)   orders: 10->1, 11->1, 12->3, 13->NULL
SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;        -- Ana 10, Ana 11, Cy 12

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;   -- + Ben NULL

SELECT c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers c
FULL JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;   -- + Ben NULL, + NULL 13

SELECT s.size, c.colour
FROM sizes s CROSS JOIN colours c;            -- every size with every colour

concepts.title: ON versus WHERE in an outer join
concepts.body: For an inner join, a condition in ON and the same condition in WHERE give the same rows. For an outer join they do not. **ON** decides which right rows count as a match; unmatched left rows are still kept. **WHERE** runs after the join, on the NULL-padded rows too, and `o.status = 'paid'` is unknown for a NULL status, so WHERE removes exactly the rows the LEFT JOIN was written to keep. The query silently becomes an inner join, and Postgres's planner will even plan it as one. Rule: filters on the **preserved** (left) table go in WHERE; filters on the **optional** (right) table go in ON. The exception is the anti-join test `WHERE o.id IS NULL`, which is deliberately applied after the join. Then count with `count(o.id)`, not `count(*)`: the NULL-padded row is one row, so `count(*)` says 1 for a customer with no orders.
concepts.code:
-- Wrong: customers without a paid order vanish
SELECT c.id, count(o.id)
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.id;

-- Right: the filter decides what matches, every customer stays
SELECT c.id, count(o.id) AS paid_orders
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
WHERE c.region = 'EU'             -- left-table filter: fine in WHERE
GROUP BY c.id;

concepts.title: Fan-out: one-to-many joins multiply rows
concepts.body: Joining `orders` to `order_items` gives one row per item, so each order's `total` is repeated once per item and `sum(o.total)` is inflated. Join two independent one-to-many tables to the same parent (items **and** payments) and you get items × payments rows per order, which breaks every count and sum. `count(DISTINCT ...)` patches counts but not sums: two different orders can share the same total. The fix is to **aggregate the many side down to the join key first**, in a subquery or CTE, so each side has one row per key, then join. A quick sanity check in an interview: compare `count(*)` of the joined result with the row count you expect at your stated grain.
concepts.code:
-- Inflated: each order total repeats once per item
SELECT sum(o.total) FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id;

-- Aggregate each child table to one row per order, then join
WITH item_counts AS (
  SELECT order_id, count(*) AS items FROM order_items GROUP BY order_id
), paid AS (
  SELECT order_id, sum(amount) AS paid FROM payments GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.id, o.total,
       coalesce(ic.items, 0) AS items,
       coalesce(p.paid, 0)   AS paid
FROM orders o
LEFT JOIN item_counts ic ON ic.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN paid p        ON p.order_id  = o.id;

concepts.title: Self joins: hierarchies and pairs
concepts.body: A self join reads the same table under two aliases, as two independent inputs. The classic use is a **hierarchy one level deep**: join `staff e` to `staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id` to put each person next to their manager; make it a LEFT JOIN or the CEO (NULL `manager_id`) disappears. Deeper levels need a recursive CTE. The other use is **pairs** of rows that share something: same team, same customer, overlapping times. An equality on the shared column alone returns each row paired with itself and every pair twice, (A,B) and (B,A). Add `a.id < b.id` to keep each unordered pair once; use `a.id <> b.id` only when ordered pairs are the point. Keep range conditions such as "within 30 days" in a form an index can use: `b.hired_on BETWEEN a.hired_on - 30 AND a.hired_on + 30` rather than wrapping both columns in `abs(...)`.
concepts.code:
-- Each person with their manager (CEO kept with NULL)
SELECT e.full_name AS person, m.full_name AS manager
FROM staff e
LEFT JOIN staff m ON m.id = e.manager_id;

-- Customers who ordered on the same day, each pair once
SELECT DISTINCT a.customer_id, b.customer_id AS other_customer, a.placed_on
FROM orders a
JOIN orders b
  ON  b.placed_on = a.placed_on
  AND a.customer_id < b.customer_id;

concepts.title: Semi joins and anti joins
concepts.body: A **semi join** asks "has at least one match": `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)` or `WHERE c.id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders)`. Each left row comes back **once**, however many matches it has, so no DISTINCT is needed; a plain JOIN would repeat it. An **anti join** asks "has no match". Write it as `NOT EXISTS (...)` or as `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.id IS NULL` (test a column that is NOT NULL in real rows, such as the primary key); Postgres plans both as a Hash or Merge Anti Join. Avoid `NOT IN (subquery)`: `x NOT IN (1, NULL)` means `x <> 1 AND x <> NULL`, which is never true, so a single NULL in the subquery returns **no rows**. Postgres cannot turn NOT IN into an anti join for that reason, so it is often slower as well as wrong. `IN` is safe: NULLs simply do not match.

concepts.title: USING, composite keys and NULL keys
concepts.body: `JOIN orders USING (customer_id)` is shorthand for equality on same-named columns, and the output has **one** `customer_id` column instead of two; in a FULL JOIN that column is `COALESCE(left.customer_id, right.customer_id)`. Use ON when the names differ or the condition is not plain equality. Avoid `NATURAL JOIN`: it joins on every same-named column, so adding `created_at` to both tables silently changes the result. When the key has several columns, every one must be in the condition, `ON a.region = b.region AND a.sku = b.sku` or `USING (region, sku)`; dropping one is a fan-out bug. NULL keys never match under `=`. If two NULLs really should pair, use `a.k IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.k`, but know that Postgres cannot use a hash or merge join for it, so prefer fixing the data or joining on `coalesce(a.k, -1) = coalesce(b.k, -1)` when a sentinel is safe.
concepts.code:
SELECT order_id, o.total, s.carrier
FROM orders_v o
JOIN shipments s USING (order_id);     -- one order_id column in the output

-- Composite key: both columns, or every SKU repeats across regions
SELECT s.region, s.sku, s.on_hand, p.price
FROM stock s
JOIN prices p ON p.region = s.region AND p.sku = s.sku;

-- NULL-safe equality (rarely what you want)
SELECT a.id, b.id
FROM shipments a
JOIN shipments b ON a.batch IS NOT DISTINCT FROM b.batch AND a.id < b.id;

example:
-- One row per customer: lifetime orders, items and money paid, without fan-out.
WITH order_stats AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id,
         count(*)                 AS orders,
         sum(o.total)             AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
), item_stats AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, sum(i.qty) AS items
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.id AS customer_id,
       c.name,
       coalesce(os.orders, 0)  AS paid_orders,
       coalesce(os.revenue, 0) AS revenue,
       coalesce(its.items, 0)  AS items
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN order_stats os ON os.customer_id = c.id
LEFT JOIN item_stats its ON its.customer_id = c.id
ORDER BY revenue DESC, customer_id;

-- Each CTE has one row per customer, so the LEFT JOINs cannot multiply rows,
-- and customers with no paid orders still appear with zeros.
task: Tables `customers(id, name, region)` and `orders(id, customer_id, status, total, placed_on)`; guest orders have a NULL `customer_id`. Build a report with **one row per customer** showing their **paid** orders placed in **calendar year 2024**. Return `customer_id`, `name`, `paid_orders` (number of such orders) and `paid_total` (sum of their `total`), in that order. Every customer appears, including those with no orders, only unpaid orders or only orders outside 2024: they get `paid_orders` = 0 and `paid_total` = 0. An order is paid only when `status = 'paid'` (NULL is not paid). Customers can share a name. Row order does not matter.
starter:
-- Paid orders placed in 2024, per customer.
-- Every customer must appear, with 0 orders and 0 total if they have none.
SELECT c.id AS customer_id, c.name, count(*) AS paid_orders, sum(o.total) AS paid_total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  AND o.placed_on >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND o.placed_on < DATE '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
hints: Run the starter on the first test and look at which customers are missing. Their joined rows have `o.status` NULL, so what does the WHERE clause do to them?
Move the status and date tests into the LEFT JOIN's ON clause, count `o.id` rather than `*`, and wrap the sum in `coalesce(..., 0)`. Group by `c.id`, not just the name.
solution:
SELECT c.id AS customer_id,
       c.name,
       count(o.id) AS paid_orders,
       coalesce(sum(o.total), 0) AS paid_total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON  o.customer_id = c.id
  AND o.status = 'paid'
  AND o.placed_on >= DATE '2024-01-01'
  AND o.placed_on <  DATE '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;

The grain is one row per customer, so `customers` is the preserved side of a LEFT JOIN. The status and date tests describe **which orders count as a match**, so they belong in ON: a customer with no qualifying order still gets one NULL-padded row. In the starter they sit in WHERE, which runs after the join and evaluates `NULL = 'paid'` as unknown, deleting every customer without a paid 2024 order. `count(o.id)` counts only real matches (the padded row contributes 0, where `count(*)` would say 1), and `sum` over no rows is NULL, so `coalesce(sum(o.total), 0)` turns it into 0. The half-open range `>= '2024-01-01' AND < '2025-01-01'` includes 31 December without worrying about time parts and lets an index on `placed_on` work. Grouping by `c.id` keeps two customers called Hal apart; Postgres allows `c.name` in the SELECT because it is functionally dependent on the primary key, but listing it in GROUP BY is portable. Guest orders never match because `NULL = c.id` is never true.
checklist: Every customer appears exactly once, including those with no orders at all.
Right-table filters (status, date range) are in ON, not WHERE.
I count `o.id`, not `*`, and the total is 0 rather than NULL for customers with no paid orders.
The date range is half-open and includes 31 December 2024 but not 1 January 2025.
I group by the customer's id, so customers with the same name are not merged.
pitfalls: Filtering the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE, which quietly turns it into an inner join.
Using `count(*)` after a LEFT JOIN: an unmatched row still counts as 1.
Summing a parent column after joining a child table, so each value is repeated once per child row.
Writing `NOT IN (subquery)` on a nullable column: one NULL makes the result empty.
Self-joining with only an equality, which returns each row paired with itself and every pair twice.
Joining on part of a composite key, or using NATURAL JOIN, and multiplying rows without noticing.
Expecting NULL keys to match each other; `NULL = NULL` is unknown.

walkthrough.title: What the engine does with a join
walkthrough.body: Postgres has three join algorithms, and knowing them answers most performance follow-ups. A **nested loop** runs the inner side once per outer row; it is fast when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index on the join key, and it is the only option for conditions like `<` or `BETWEEN` without an index. A **hash join** builds an in-memory hash table on one input and probes it with the other, reading each once; it needs an equality condition. A **merge join** walks two inputs sorted on the key. Run `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` and you will see `Hash Join`, `Hash Left Join`, `Hash Anti Join` or `Nested Loop`. Two practical facts: Postgres does **not** index foreign-key columns automatically, so `orders(customer_id)` usually needs its own index; and the planner reorders inner joins freely (up to `join_collapse_limit`, 8 by default) but must respect the semantics of outer joins.
walkthrough.code:
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT c.id, count(o.id)
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
GROUP BY c.id;
-- Look for: Hash Right Join / Hash Left Join, actual rows vs estimated rows

walkthrough.title: Solve the task in three moves
walkthrough.body: First, say the grain out loud: "one row per customer, so customers is the preserved side of a LEFT JOIN." Second, sort every condition into ON or WHERE: status and date describe which orders match, so ON; there is no customer filter, so no WHERE at all. Third, aggregate safely: `count(o.id)` so the padded row counts 0, `coalesce(sum(o.total), 0)`, and `GROUP BY c.id`. Then test it mentally on the three awkward customers: no orders, only a pending order, and an order dated 2025-01-01. If any of them is missing, a right-table test has leaked into WHERE.

walkthrough.title: Choosing a form for "has" and "has not"
walkthrough.body: When the question is about existence, do not reach for JOIN plus DISTINCT. "Customers who bought something" is a semi join: `EXISTS`, or `IN` on a subquery, each returns every customer once and lets the planner stop at the first match. "Customers who never bought" is an anti join: `NOT EXISTS` is the clearest and is NULL-safe; `LEFT JOIN ... WHERE o.id IS NULL` is equivalent and handy when you also want columns from a third table. Reserve `NOT IN` for a literal list you control, such as `status NOT IN ('refunded', 'void')`, and remember that even then a NULL `status` row is filtered out, because `NULL NOT IN (...)` is unknown.

extraPractice.title: Products never ordered
extraPractice.prompt: Tables `products(id, sku, name)` and `order_lines(id, order_id, product_id, qty)`. Custom, made-to-order lines have a NULL `product_id`, and a line may reference a product id that has since been deleted. Return `product_id` and `sku` for every product that appears on **no** order line. Row order does not matter.
hints: The starter uses `NOT IN (SELECT product_id ...)`. What is `2 NOT IN (1, NULL)`?
Use `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_lines l WHERE l.product_id = p.id)`, or a LEFT JOIN with `WHERE l.id IS NULL`.
extraPractice.solution:
SELECT p.id AS product_id, p.sku
FROM products p
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1
  FROM order_lines l
  WHERE l.product_id = p.id
);

`NOT EXISTS` asks, for each product, whether any line matches; a NULL `product_id` matches nothing, so it is ignored instead of poisoning the whole result as it does with `NOT IN`. Lines for deleted products also match nothing. Postgres plans this as a Hash Anti Join, reading each table once.
checklist: A NULL `product_id` on any line does not empty the result.
A product ordered many times is excluded once, not checked per line.
With no order lines at all, every product is returned.

extraPractice.title: Teammates hired close together
extraPractice.prompt: Tables `teams(id, name)` and `staff(id, full_name, team_id, hired_on)`; unassigned contractors have a NULL `team_id`. Find every pair of people in the **same team** whose hire dates are **at most 30 days apart** (30 counts). Return `team` (the team name), `first_id`, `second_id` and `days_apart`, where `first_id` is the smaller staff id of the pair and `days_apart` is never negative. List each pair once, never pair a person with themselves, and leave unassigned staff out. Sort by `team`, then `first_id`, then `second_id`.
hints: Self-join `staff a JOIN staff b ON b.team_id = a.team_id`. Which extra condition removes both self-pairs and the mirrored (B, A) copy of each pair?

In Postgres, `date - date` is an integer number of days. Write the window as `b.hired_on BETWEEN a.hired_on - 30 AND a.hired_on + 30` so an index on `(team_id, hired_on)` can serve it, and report `abs(a.hired_on - b.hired_on)`.
extraPractice.solution:
SELECT t.name AS team,
       a.id AS first_id,
       b.id AS second_id,
       abs(a.hired_on - b.hired_on) AS days_apart
FROM staff a
JOIN staff b
  ON  b.team_id = a.team_id
  AND a.id < b.id
  AND b.hired_on BETWEEN a.hired_on - 30 AND a.hired_on + 30
JOIN teams t ON t.id = a.team_id
ORDER BY team, first_id, second_id;

`a.id < b.id` keeps one orientation of each pair and drops self-pairs in one condition. NULL team ids never satisfy `b.team_id = a.team_id`, so contractors drop out without an explicit test. Subtracting dates gives whole days in Postgres, so leap years are handled for you: 1 February to 2 March is 30 days in 2024 and 29 in 2023. The BETWEEN form keeps `b.hired_on` bare, which lets the planner use an index on `staff(team_id, hired_on)` for the inner side of a nested loop instead of comparing every pair in the team.
checklist: Each pair appears once, with the smaller id first, and nobody is paired with themselves.
Hires exactly 30 days apart are included; 31 days apart are not.
Staff with a NULL team never appear, and a team with one person produces no rows.
The result is ordered by team, first_id, second_id.

followUps.question: The report is slow on 50 million orders. What do you look at?
followUps.answer: Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` and compare estimated with actual rows at each node. Make sure `orders(customer_id)` is indexed, since Postgres does not index foreign keys automatically; for this filter, a composite or partial index such as `(customer_id) WHERE status = 'paid'` or `(status, placed_on, customer_id)` helps. For a whole-table report a hash join over a sequential scan is often right, so the bigger win may be pre-aggregating orders per customer in a CTE before the join, or a summary table refreshed incrementally.

followUps.question: NOT EXISTS, LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL or NOT IN: which do you use?
followUps.answer: NOT EXISTS by default: it states the intent, is NULL-safe and Postgres plans it as an anti join. LEFT JOIN with `WHERE right.pk IS NULL` is equivalent and also becomes an anti join; test a non-nullable column of the right table. NOT IN is wrong when the subquery can yield NULL and cannot be planned as an anti join, so it falls back to a hashed or plain subplan; if you must use it, add `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` inside the subquery and make the column NOT NULL.

followUps.question: Your SUM doubled after adding a join to `payments`. How do you explain and fix it?
followUps.answer: Orders to payments is one-to-many, so each order row is repeated once per payment and anything summed from orders or from a second child table is multiplied. State the grain, then aggregate each child table to one row per order (or per customer) in its own CTE or a LATERAL subquery and join those. `count(DISTINCT)` can patch counts but not sums.

followUps.question: Does the order you write the tables in matter?
followUps.answer: For inner joins, no: the planner considers join orders itself (exhaustively up to `join_collapse_limit` tables, 8 by default; beyond about 12 it switches to the genetic optimizer, GEQO). For outer joins, the order is part of the meaning: `a LEFT JOIN b` keeps a's rows, and a later inner join to a table reached through b can drop them again. Write the preserved table first and LEFT JOIN outwards from it.

takeaways: A join emits one row per matching pair: unmatched rows vanish in INNER, are NULL-padded in outer joins, and NULL keys never match.
In a LEFT JOIN, filters on the right table go in ON; in WHERE they turn it into an inner join. Count `right.id`, not `*`.
One-to-many joins multiply rows: aggregate the many side to the join key before joining.
Self joins need two aliases; `a.id < b.id` gives each unordered pair once with no self-pairs.
Use EXISTS for has, NOT EXISTS for has-not; NOT IN returns nothing when the subquery yields a NULL.

diagrams.title: A join matches rows, one output row per match
diagrams.alt: Flow diagram matching customer rows to order rows. Ana (id 1) matches orders 10 and 11 and produces two result rows. Cy (id 3) matches order 12 and produces one row. Ben (id 2) matches nothing; an inner join drops him and a LEFT JOIN keeps one row for him with NULL order columns. Order 13 has a NULL customer_id and matches nobody.
diagrams.caption: Count matches, not circles: each matching pair becomes a row, a left row with no match disappears in an INNER JOIN and is NULL-padded in a LEFT JOIN, and NULL keys match nothing.

steps.text: Ana's id matches two orders, so she appears in **two** result rows. One-to-many joins repeat the left row once per match.
Cy matches exactly one order: one row.
Ben matches nothing. `INNER JOIN` drops him; `LEFT JOIN` keeps one row with every `orders` column NULL. Order 13 has a NULL key, which equals nothing, so only a `RIGHT` or `FULL` join would show it.

diagrams.title: Filtering the right table in WHERE versus ON
diagrams.alt: Comparison for a customer with no paid orders. On the left, the LEFT JOIN keeps Ben with NULL order columns, then WHERE o.status = 'paid' evaluates NULL = 'paid' as unknown and drops Ben, so the report silently becomes an inner join. On the right, the status test lives in ON, Ben keeps his NULL-padded row, and count(o.id) reports 0.
diagrams.caption: ON decides which rows match; WHERE runs after the join and discards NULL-padded rows. Put right-table filters of a LEFT JOIN in ON.

diagrams.title: SUM(total) for three orders of 100 with 1, 2 and 4 items
diagrams.alt: Bar chart of revenue for three orders worth 100 each that have 1, 2 and 4 line items. The true sum is 300. Joining orders to items first and then summing the order total gives 700 because each total is repeated once per item. Aggregating items per order first and then joining gives 300 again.
diagrams.caption: The 700 is exact, not illustrative: each order total is counted once per matching item. Aggregate the many side to the join key's grain before joining.

diagrams.title: Self join: from 9 combinations to 3 unique pairs
diagrams.alt: Flow diagram of a self join on a staff table with rows A, B and C. Aliases a and b both read the same three rows and combine into nine pairs. Three are self-pairs where a.id equals b.id, three are mirror pairs where a.id is greater than b.id, and the filter a.id < b.id keeps the three unique pairs.
diagrams.caption: Alias the table twice and add a.id < b.id: it removes self-pairs and mirror duplicates in one condition.

steps.text: Two aliases of the same table are two independent row sources. With only an equality on `team_id`, every row pairs with every teammate, itself included.
A row always matches itself: Ada is hired 0 days after Ada. `a.id <> b.id` removes these.
`<>` still returns (A,B) and (B,A). For unordered pairs that is a duplicate.
`a.id < b.id` keeps exactly one orientation of each pair and no self-pairs: n(n-1)/2 rows per group.

diagrams.title: NOT IN versus NOT EXISTS when the subquery has a NULL
diagrams.alt: Comparison of two anti joins for products never ordered when one order line has a NULL product_id. On the left, NOT IN expands to a chain of inequalities that includes 2 <> NULL, which is unknown, so no product is returned. On the right, NOT EXISTS asks whether any matching line exists; the NULL line matches nothing, so unordered products are returned.
diagrams.caption: NOT IN is three-valued: one NULL in the list makes it never true. NOT EXISTS only asks whether a match exists.

diagrams.title: How Postgres runs a hash join for customers LEFT JOIN orders
diagrams.alt: Sequence diagram of a hash join. The planner chooses a hash join. The orders scan reads every order and inserts it into an in-memory hash table keyed by customer_id. The customers scan then probes the hash table with each customer id. Matches are emitted as joined rows, and a customer with no match is emitted once with NULL order columns because it is a LEFT JOIN.
diagrams.caption: A hash join reads each input once: build a hash table on one side, probe it with the other. Equality join keys make this possible, which is why = joins scale and inequality joins often do not.

messages.label: Hash Join: build on orders
messages.note: Using row estimates, the planner puts the input it expects to be smaller on the build side, which must fit in work_mem or spill to batches.

messages.label: insert by customer_id
messages.note: One pass over orders. A NULL key can never satisfy =, so it can never be found by a probe.

messages.label: one row per matching order
messages.note: Two matching orders produce two rows: this is where fan-out happens.

messages.label: no match: emit with NULLs
messages.note: Only because it is a LEFT JOIN with customers preserved. With orders hashed and customers probing, EXPLAIN shows Hash Left Join; if the planner hashes customers instead, it shows Hash Right Join.

exercises.starter:
-- Paid orders placed in 2024, per customer.
-- Every customer must appear, with 0 orders and 0 total if they have none.
SELECT c.id AS customer_id, c.name, count(*) AS paid_orders, sum(o.total) AS paid_total
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid'
  AND o.placed_on >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND o.placed_on < DATE '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name;
exercises.solution:
SELECT c.id AS customer_id,
       c.name,
       count(o.id) AS paid_orders,
       coalesce(sum(o.total), 0) AS paid_total
FROM customers c

exercises.starter:
-- Same-team pairs hired at most 30 days apart, each pair once.
SELECT t.name AS team, a.id AS first_id, b.id AS second_id,
       abs(a.hired_on - b.hired_on) AS days_apart
FROM staff a
JOIN staff b ON b.team_id = a.team_id
JOIN teams t ON t.id = a.team_id
WHERE abs(a.hired_on - b.hired_on) <= 30
ORDER BY team, first_id, second_id;
exercises.solution:
SELECT t.name AS team,
       a.id AS first_id,
       b.id AS second_id,
       abs(a.hired_on - b.hired_on) AS days_apart
FROM staff a
JOIN staff b
  ON  b.team_id = a.team_id
  AND a.id < b.id
  AND b.hired_on BETWEEN a.hired_on - 30 AND a.hired_on + 30
JOIN teams t ON t.id = a.team_id
ORDER BY team, first_id, second_id;

predict.code:
WITH product(id) AS (VALUES (1), (2), (3)),
     line(product_id) AS (VALUES (1), (NULL))
SELECT count(*)
FROM product
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT product_id FROM line);
predict.explain: `2 NOT IN (1, NULL)` means `2 <> 1 AND 2 <> NULL`, which is `true AND unknown` = unknown, and WHERE keeps only true. One NULL in the subquery empties the result. `NOT EXISTS` returns 2.

predict.code:
WITH customer(id) AS (VALUES (1), (2)),
     orders(customer_id, status) AS (VALUES (1, 'paid'), (2, 'refunded'))
SELECT count(*)
FROM customer c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'paid';
predict.explain: Customer 2 survives the LEFT JOIN with its refunded order, then WHERE removes it. Had customer 2 had no order, its NULL-extended row would fail `NULL = 'paid'` too. A WHERE test on the right table turns the outer join into an inner join; put it in ON.

predict.code:
WITH orders(id, total) AS (VALUES (1, 100), (2, 50)),
     items(order_id) AS (VALUES (1), (1), (1), (2))
SELECT sum(o.total)
FROM orders o
JOIN items i ON i.order_id = o.id;
predict.explain: Order 1 matches three item rows, so its 100 is repeated three times: 300 + 50 = 350. Joining one-to-many before summing a column of the one side inflates the sum.

predict.code:
WITH a(k) AS (VALUES (1), (NULL)),
     b(k) AS (VALUES (1), (NULL))
SELECT count(*)
FROM a
JOIN b ON a.k = b.k;
predict.explain: `NULL = NULL` is unknown, not true, so the NULL keys never match. Use `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` only if NULLs really should pair up.

predict.code:
WITH a(id, x) AS (VALUES (1, 'a'), (2, 'b')),
     b(id, y) AS (VALUES (2, 'B'), (3, 'C'))
SELECT id, x, y
FROM a
FULL JOIN b USING (id)
ORDER BY id;
choices:
1 | a | NULL
2 | b | B
3 | NULL | C

1 | a | NULL
2 | b | B
NULL | NULL | C
predict.explain: With `USING`, the output has one `id` column, which for a FULL JOIN is `COALESCE(a.id, b.id)`. With `ON a.id = b.id` and `SELECT a.id`, the third row would show NULL.

predict.code:
WITH staff(id) AS (VALUES (1), (2), (3), (4))
SELECT
  (SELECT count(*) FROM staff a JOIN staff b ON a.id <> b.id) AS ordered_pairs,
  (SELECT count(*) FROM staff a JOIN staff b ON a.id < b.id) AS unique_pairs;
predict.explain: Four rows give 16 combinations; `<>` drops the 4 self-pairs, leaving 12 ordered pairs where (1,2) and (2,1) both appear. `<` keeps one of each: 4 × 3 / 2 = 6.

lab.tip: Before typing, say the grain and the preserved side: "one row per customer, so customers LEFT JOIN orders, and every condition about orders goes in ON." Then name the edge rows you will check: a customer with no orders, a NULL key, and a parent with several children. Interviewers are listening for fan-out and the ON/WHERE trap more than for syntax.
